Least squares as a projection, for programmers

Why linear regression has a closed form: the column space, orthogonal projection and the normal equations (via orthogonality and via the gradient), the hat matrix, how it is really solved (QR, SVD, and why not to invert XᵀX), R² as a squared cosine, multicollinearity and ridge, weighted least squares, maximum likelihood and robustness. With a from-scratch module verified against NumPy and scikit-learn, a simulated fleet and a worked example by hand.

Summary

  • is the orthogonal projection of onto the column space of . The residual is orthogonal to every column: , the normal equations.
  • is symmetric and idempotent, with trace . is a Pythagorean decomposition.
  • You don't invert : its condition number is . Use QR () or SVD (pseudoinverse); np.linalg.lstsq uses SVD.
  • is the squared cosine between centered and its projection, and it never drops when you add columns: measure out of sample.
  • With nearly collinear columns, blows up (VIF). Ridge, , stabilizes it.
  • With Gaussian noise, least squares (weighted if the variance changes) is maximum likelihood; with outliers, a robust loss (Huber) is better.
‖y − Xβ‖²→ projection onto col(X)→ Xᵀr = 0→ QR / SVD→ R², VIF→ ridge, WLS, Huber

§1 · Setup

A distance problem in

With observations and columns (including the column of ones for the intercept), , , the least squares problem is

The key is to switch viewpoints: instead of points in , look at a single vector in (one axis per observation). Each is a linear combination of the columns, so the set of possible predictions is the column space , a subspace of dimension (the map from topic 3, and its image). The problem is: the point of a subspace closest to .

Projection theorem. That point exists, is unique, and is the only with . Proof: if is orthogonal to the subspace and is any other point in it, lies in the subspace and, by Pythagoras,

with equality only if . It's the shadow of a vector on a line from topic 2, generalized to a subspace. With a single column , the projection is : the best constant is the mean. The uniqueness is of ; that of also requires the columns to be independent (§2).

Linear and polynomial regression in the ML series uses this solution; here we care about the why. A polynomial regression is the same thing with columns : it is still linear in , and that's all it takes for the solution to be a projection.

§2 · Normal equations

Two roads to the same system: orthogonality and the gradient

Via orthogonality. is equivalent to being orthogonal to each column, for all , that is:

Via the gradient. The objective function is a quadratic:

with

The Hessian is positive semidefinite (), so is convex and every point with zero gradient is a global minimum: the same equations. If has full rank , is positive definite, invertible, and

That's the "closed form"; gradient descent walks the same quadratic in steps, and its speed depends on , the same number that will show up in §3. If the rank is less than (a column is a combination of others), there are infinitely many with the same ; the pseudoinverse picks the minimum-norm one.

The hat matrix (it "puts the hat" on ) is the orthogonal projector onto :

Projecting twice is projecting once (idempotent), and the projection is orthogonal (symmetric). The eigenvalues are 0 or 1, and the trace counts the ones: the dimension of the subspace. projects onto the orthogonal complement, of dimension , where the residual lives. The diagonal is the leverage of observation : . Observations with extreme have high leverage and drag the line (idea 1 of the simple version). If there is an intercept, and : the residuals sum to zero.

§3 · How it's really solved

QR, SVD, and why not to invert XᵀX

QR. With the reduced factorization ( with orthonormal columns, upper triangular), , and

which is solved by back substitution. is obtained with Householder reflections (stable, about flops) or with modified Gram–Schmidt (topic 2). SVD. With ,

More expensive, but it gives the minimum-norm solution under rank deficiency and shows where the problem is: a small divides and amplifies the noise in . This is what np.linalg.lstsq does (LAPACK gelsd), with rcond as ; scikit-learn's LinearRegression calls scipy.linalg.lstsq.

Why not the normal equations. The condition number measures how much relative errors get amplified. Since ,

In double precision (), solving the normal equations loses on the order of digits; QR and SVD, on the order of when the residual is small (with a large residual, the term shows up in any method; Golub and Van Loan, §5.3). Forming also loses the information in the columns below . The experiment in §8 (precision.py) builds with a controlled and a known exact solution:

§4 · Interpretation

R² is a squared cosine, and it always goes up

With an intercept, and, subtracting from everything, Pythagoras gives the sum-of-squares decomposition:

where is the angle between and . Since the cosine of centered vectors is the Pearson correlation (topic 2), ; with a single regressor, . Without an intercept the decomposition doesn't hold with , and the usual can come out negative or mislead.

Degrees of freedom. If with , , then and

The residual lives in a subspace of dimension : each column "eats" one dimension of the noise. Monotonicity: if you add a column, the new column space contains the old one, and the projection onto a bigger subspace can't end up farther away: never goes up and never goes down, even if the column is noise. With independent columns, and . Adjusted , , partly corrects for this; the honest answer is to measure on held-out data (topic 1 of Preparing the data). In idea 4 of the simple version, with 30 trips, adding 25 noise columns lowers the training RMSE from 1.14 to 0.43 L/100 km and raises the test RMSE from 1.47 to 4.13.

§5 · Multicollinearity

When the column space is poorly anchored

Under the model of §4, is unbiased and

If two columns are nearly collinear, there is a tiny whose points in the "one goes up, the other goes down" direction: the variance in that direction blows up while barely changes, because the column space is almost the same. Per column, with the of regressing on the others:

A VIF of 10 multiplies the standard deviation by ; in the fleet of §8 (load and total weight with nearly constant tare) the VIF is 1,806. What is well determined is the linear combination the column space "sees" (in §8, the sum of the two coefficients). Remedies: drop or combine columns, collect data where the columns separate, or regularize. Ridge (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970):

Directions with are left intact and those with are switched off: you trade a little bias for much less variance. The effective degrees of freedom are . It is equivalent to least squares with extra rows and zeros in , which is how ridge in §7 implements it (with QR, without forming ). In practice: don't penalize the intercept (center), standardize first because the penalty depends on the units, and choose by cross-validation (RidgeCV).

§6 · Weights, likelihood and robustness

Weighted least squares, Gaussians and Huber

Weighted. If each observation has its own variance, (short trips whose fuel use is measured with more noise than long ones, different sensors), you minimize

which is ordinary least squares on the rows scaled by : an orthogonal projection with the inner product . It's sample_weight in scikit-learn.

Maximum likelihood. If independent, the log-likelihood is

and maximizing it in is minimizing the sum of squares: least squares is the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimator (with unequal variances, the weighted one). Without assuming normality, the Gauss–Markov theorem guarantees it is the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator if the errors are uncorrelated and homoscedastic. The connection with likelihood and distributions is developed in topic 14 of this collection.

Robustness. The squared loss is the likelihood of a Gaussian, which has almost no tails: an outlier is treated as impossible and drags the fit. Huber (1964) uses if and outside: quadratic in the middle and linear in the tails. It is solved by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), with : each iteration is a weighted projection. In §8, with 4 of 60 flow meter readings shifted by 25 L/100 km, OLS gives an intercept of 15.9 (truth: 18) and Huber, 18.8. Before choosing a loss, it pays to detect and understand the outliers.

§7 · From scratch

Normal equations, Householder, SVD and ridge, verified

mcuadrados.py

"""Least squares from scratch: normal equations, QR (Householder), SVD and ridge."""
import numpy as np

def con_intercepto(X):
    """Prepends a column of ones (the intercept term)."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float)
    return np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]

def normales(X, y):
    """Solves XᵀX β = Xᵀy. Fast, but squares the condition number."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)

def householder_qr(X):
    """Reduced QR with Householder reflections: X = Q R, Q (n×p) orthonormal, R (p×p) upper triangular."""
    A = np.array(X, float); n, p = A.shape
    Q = np.eye(n)
    for k in range(p):
        x = A[k:, k]
        v = x.copy(); s = 1.0 if x[0] >= 0 else -1.0
        v[0] += s * np.linalg.norm(x)                  # v = x + sign(x₁)‖x‖e₁ (avoids cancellation)
        nv = np.linalg.norm(v)
        if nv == 0:
            continue
        v /= nv
        A[k:, :] -= 2.0 * np.outer(v, v @ A[k:, :])    # H = I − 2vvᵀ applied to the submatrix
        Q[:, k:] -= 2.0 * np.outer(Q[:, k:] @ v, v)    # accumulates Q = H₁ H₂ … H_p
    return Q[:, :p], np.triu(A[:p, :])

def resolver_triangular(R, b):
    """Back substitution for R β = b."""
    p = len(b); beta = np.zeros(p)
    for i in range(p - 1, -1, -1):
        beta[i] = (b[i] - R[i, i + 1:] @ beta[i + 1:]) / R[i, i]
    return beta

def mc_qr(X, y):
    """β = R⁻¹ Qᵀ y: doesn't form XᵀX, so the error depends on cond(X), not cond(X)²."""
    Q, R = householder_qr(X)
    return resolver_triangular(R, Q.T @ np.asarray(y, float))

def mc_svd(X, y, rcond=None):
    """Pseudoinverse: β = V Σ⁺ Uᵀ y. Drops singular values < rcond·σ_max (minimum-norm solution)."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float); U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
    rcond = np.finfo(float).eps * max(X.shape) if rcond is None else rcond
    keep = s > rcond * s[0]
    return Vt[keep].T @ ((U[:, keep].T @ np.asarray(y, float)) / s[keep])

def ridge(X, y, lam, intercepto=True):
    """Ridge: minimizes ‖y − b₀ − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖² (intercept not penalized). Returns (b₀, β)."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    if intercepto:
        mx, my = X.mean(0), y.mean(); Xc, yc = X - mx, y - my
    else:
        mx, my, Xc, yc = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0, X, y
    # as augmented least squares: [Xc; √λ I] β ≈ [yc; 0], solved by QR
    A = np.r_[Xc, np.sqrt(lam) * np.eye(X.shape[1])]; b = np.r_[yc, np.zeros(X.shape[1])]
    beta = mc_qr(A, b)
    return my - mx @ beta, beta

def sombrero(X):
    """H = X (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ = Q Qᵀ. Projects y onto the column space of X."""
    Q, _ = householder_qr(X)
    return Q @ Q.T

def r2(y, yhat):
    y = np.asarray(y, float); r = y - yhat; d = y - y.mean()
    return 1.0 - (r @ r) / (d @ d)

def vif(X):
    """Variance inflation factor of each column: 1 / (1 − R²_j), with R²_j from regressing x_j on the others."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float); out = []
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        otras = con_intercepto(np.delete(X, j, axis=1))
        b = mc_qr(otras, X[:, j]); out.append(1.0 / (1.0 - r2(X[:, j], otras @ b)))
    return np.array(out)

def ponderados(X, y, w):
    """Weighted least squares: minimizes Σ wᵢ (yᵢ − xᵢβ)². Same as scaling each row by √wᵢ."""
    sw = np.sqrt(np.asarray(w, float))
    return mc_qr(np.asarray(X, float) * sw[:, None], np.asarray(y, float) * sw)

check.py · 200 random problems (n from 8 to 59, p from 1 to 6 plus intercept) · actual output

The errors are on the order of : rounding differences between implementations, because these problems are well conditioned (§8 shows what happens when they aren't). The Householder QR matches np.linalg.qr up to the sign of each column of (and row of ), which is arbitrary. The avoids subtracting two nearly equal numbers. In the rank-deficient case, mc_svd gives the same minimum-norm solution as lstsq.

§8 · In the fleet

Fuel use, load and total weight: twin columns and bad readings

We simulate trips with

where the total weight is the tare (14 t with a standard deviation of 150 kg) plus the load (2 to 24 t). The model gets load and total weight.

flota.py

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor
from mcuadrados import con_intercepto, normales, mc_qr, mc_svd, ridge, r2, vif

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
def viajes(n):
    """Fuel use (L/100 km) from total weight and the average grade of the route."""
    tara = 14.0 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, n)          # nearly all trucks weigh the same when empty
    carga = rng.uniform(2, 24, n); peso = tara + carga
    pend = rng.uniform(-1, 3, n)                   # average % uphill grade of the route
    cons = 18.0 + 0.5 * peso + 2.0 * pend + rng.normal(0, 1.5, n)
    return np.c_[carga, peso, pend], cons
X, y = viajes(400); Xte, yte = viajes(2000)
A = con_intercepto(X)
print("cond(X) =", f"{np.linalg.cond(A):.0f}", " cond(XᵀX) =", f"{np.linalg.cond(A.T @ A):.1e}")
print("VIF load, weight, grade:", vif(X).round(0))
for nom, f in [("normal", normales), ("QR", mc_qr), ("SVD", mc_svd)]:
    b = f(A, y); rm = np.sqrt(np.mean((yte - con_intercepto(Xte) @ b) ** 2))
    print(f"{nom:9s}", b.round(3), " load+weight =", round(b[1] + b[2], 3), " test RMSE", round(rm, 3))
# what isn't known is the split between load and weight: 8 weeks of 50 trips each
print("week     load  weight    sum   (least squares)     |  ridge λ=10: load  weight")
for s in range(8):
    Xs, ys = viajes(50); b = mc_qr(con_intercepto(Xs), ys); b0, br = ridge(Xs, ys, 10.0)
    print(f"{s + 1:4d}   {b[1]:6.2f}  {b[2]:6.2f}  {b[1] + b[2]:5.2f}                       |  {br[0]:6.2f} {br[1]:6.2f}")
# drop the redundant column: stable and just as good
B = con_intercepto(X[:, 1:]); b = mc_qr(B, y)
print("weight and grade only:", b.round(3), " test RMSE", round(np.sqrt(np.mean((yte - con_intercepto(Xte[:, 1:]) @ b) ** 2)), 3))
# robustness: 4 trips with a broken flow meter (reads 25 L/100 km too high)
Xo, yo = viajes(60); yo[:4] += 25
bo = mc_qr(con_intercepto(Xo[:, 1:]), yo); hb = HuberRegressor(epsilon=1.35, alpha=0).fit(Xo[:, 1:], yo)
print("with 4 bad readings  LS:", bo.round(2), " Huber:", np.r_[hb.intercept_, hb.coef_].round(2), " (truth: 18, 0.5, 2)")

With the three methods agree on every digit shown: the problem isn't numerical but statistical. The VIF of 1,806 says the standard deviation of each coefficient is times what it would be without its twin. Week to week, the load coefficient ranges from −1.04 to 1.67 (the truth is 0), while the sum stays between 0.44 and 0.57 (truth 0.5) and the test RMSE is 1.49, the noise level. Ridge with stabilizes the split (0.19 to 0.36), biased toward splitting it down the middle: it can't know which of the two matters, because the data don't say. Dropping the redundant column is the cleanest: same RMSE and coefficients close to the truth.

import numpy as np
from mcuadrados import normales, mc_qr, mc_svd

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, p = 200, 6
U, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, p))); V, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(p, p)))
beta = rng.normal(size=p)
print("cond(X)   cond(XᵀX)     normal error   QR error    SVD error   lstsq error")
for k in [2, 4, 6, 7, 8]:
    s = np.logspace(0, -k, p)                      # singular values from 1 to 10^-k
    X = U @ np.diag(s) @ V.T; y = X @ beta         # consistent system: the exact solution is beta

§9 · Checklist

Before you trust a least squares fit

  • Solve with lstsq, QR or a library solver; never inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y.
  • Look at and the VIFs; scale columns with very different units and center polynomials.
  • Check and that the residuals sum to 0 with an intercept: if not, there's an implementation bug.
  • Measure the error on held-out data; don't choose columns by training .
  • With nearly collinear columns, don't interpret individual coefficients: drop, combine or use ridge (standardized, by cross-validation).
  • Plot residuals against predictions and against each column: curvature (a term is missing), funnel (non-constant variance: use weights).
  • Look for observations with high leverage and a large residual; if there are impossible readings, clean them or use Huber.
  • If the system doesn't fit in memory, accumulate and with scaled columns, or use blocked QR.

§10 · Worked example

Three trips, one line and a right angle

The mean as a projection, 2×2 normal equations, orthogonal residuals, R² as a cosine and the hat matrix, by hand and with the numbers from the simple version.

The situation. The fleet manager has three trips by the same truck with different loads and wants to know how much each tonne adds to fuel use, how much the load explains and how much noise is left. That's very little data, and precisely for that reason all the math fits on one sheet.

Example map

The three trips from idea 2 of the simple version: loads of 4, 12 and 20 tonnes and fuel use of 26, 33 and 34 L/100 km. We compute the best constant by hand, set up and solve the normal equations of the line, check that the residual is orthogonal to the columns, get R² as a squared cosine and read the hat matrix.

  1. A single number: the mean is the projection onto (1, 1, 1).
  2. The matrix X and the normal equations.
  3. Solving the 2×2 system.
  4. Predictions, residuals and the check Xᵀr = 0.
  5. Pythagoras and R² as a squared cosine.
  6. Hat matrix, leverages and noise variance.

  1. A single number: the mean is the projection onto (1, 1, 1)

    In words

    The poorest model predicts the same fuel use for all three trips. Its possible predictions are the multiples of : a line in . The best one is the projection of onto that line, using the shadow formula from topic 2.

    The math

    Where does the formula come from?

    The projection of onto the line of is . With , the numerator is the sum of the data and the denominator is how many there are: the mean. The 38 is the sum of squares around the mean (SST), which will serve as the reference for R².

    What it means: the best constant prediction is the mean, 31 L/100 km, and its errors add up to 0 (they are orthogonal to ). Any other number gives a sum of squares larger than 38: with 27, for example, 1 + 36 + 49 = 86.

  2. The matrix X and the normal equations

    In words

    Now the model is . Each row of is a trip: a 1 (so that always comes in) and its load. The normal equations require the residual to be orthogonal to both columns.

    The data

    tripload (t)fuelload²load × fuel
    142616104
    21233144396
    32034400680
    sum (3 trips)36935601,180

    What is each number?

    31·1 + 1·1 + 1·1: the number of trips
    36dot product of the column of ones with the load column: the sum of the loads
    560load · load: the sum of the squared loads
    93ones · fuel: the sum of the fuel readings
    1,180load · fuel: the sum of the products

    Each entry of and is a dot product between columns. That's why, for least squares with millions of rows, it's enough to accumulate these sums: is only .

  3. Solving the 2×2 system

    In words

    Two equations, two unknowns. With Cramer's rule: each unknown is a ratio of determinants.

    The math

    Check with the centered formula

    Subtracting from the second equation the first one multiplied by 12 (the mean load, ) gives the familiar formula, with centered sums:

    The determinant 384 is : it vanishes if all the loads are equal (the two columns would be parallel).

    What it means: fuel use . Each tonne adds half a liter per 100 km and, empty, the truck would burn 25 L/100 km (an extrapolation: no trip was empty).

  4. Predictions, residuals and the check Xᵀr = 0

    The math

    Why do they have to come out as zeros?

    Because that's the definition of the solution: is the normal equations rewritten. If either were not 0, moving or in the direction of that product would lower the sum of squares. In code, with floats, they come out around , not exactly zero.

    What it means: the residual is perpendicular to the plane of possible predictions. The sum of squares drops from 38 (constant) to 6 (line).

  5. Pythagoras and R² as a squared cosine

    In words

    We center everything by subtracting the mean, 31. The centered data vector splits into two perpendicular pieces: what the line explains, and the residual.

    The math

    Why do they match?

    The residual is orthogonal to (which lies in the plane), so the dot product of the two centered vectors is the squared length of the second one:

    So . Since, as in topic 2, the cosine of centered vectors is the Pearson correlation, is the squared correlation between actual and predicted fuel use.

    What it means: load explains 84% of the variation in fuel use on these three trips. With so little data, that number is fragile: with 2 trips, any line would pass through both and give .

  6. Hat matrix, leverages and noise variance

    In words

    turns the data into predictions: . Its diagonal, the leverage , says how much the prediction for trip depends on its own data point.

    The math (simple line)

    Where does each term come from?

    is what each data point contributes to the mean (the intercept). is what it contributes to the slope: more the further the trip is from the mean load (12 t); is the sum of those squared distances. The trace of a projection is the dimension of the space it projects onto: 2 parameters. That's why we divide by : 2 of the 3 dimensions have been "spent" on fitting, and the residual lives in just 1.

    What it means: the trips at the ends have leverage 0.83: their own fuel reading decides 83% of their prediction, like the odd trip in idea 1 of the simple version, which moved the line like a lever. The estimated noise is L/100 km, with a single degree of freedom: a very unreliable estimate. With 30 trips there would be 28.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import numpy as np
from mcuadrados import con_intercepto, normales, sombrero, r2

carga = np.array([4.0, 12.0, 20.0]); y = np.array([26.0, 33.0, 34.0])
uno = np.ones(3)
media = (y @ uno) / (uno @ uno); e0 = y - media * uno
print(media, e0, e0 @ uno, e0 @ e0)                     # the mean is the shadow of y on (1, 1, 1)
X = con_intercepto(carga)
print(X.T @ X, X.T @ y, np.linalg.det(X.T @ X).round(6))
b = normales(X, y); yhat = X @ b; r = y - yhat
print(b.round(10), yhat.round(10), r.round(10), (X.T @ r).round(10) + 0.0, round(r @ r, 10))
yc, hc = y - y.mean(), yhat - y.mean()
print(yc @ yc, round(hc @ hc, 10), round((yc @ hc) / np.sqrt((yc @ yc) * (hc @ hc)), 4), round(r2(y, yhat), 4))
H = sombrero(X); print(np.diag(H).round(4), H.trace().round(10), round((r @ r) / (3 - 2), 10))

What would change in a real system

  • Many more trips: with a large , and the coefficient intervals are reliable.
  • More columns: grade, speed, temperature; the normal equations are and are solved by QR.
  • Diagnostics: leverages and residuals to find trips that single-handedly decide the fit.
  • Validation: the error is measured on trips that weren't used for fitting.
